title: After the Decision — 선택한 뒤에 [중3·자작]
topic: 고등학교 선택 후의 불안과 작은 준비 (자작 이야기)
source_body:
I finally chose a high school last Friday. It had a science club I wanted to join, and I could get there by bus in twenty minutes. I had compared schools, talked with my parents, and visited the school. Still, I did not feel as relieved as I had expected.

That evening, my best friend told me she had chosen a different school. Suddenly, I pictured myself eating lunch alone. What if everyone else made friends quickly? What if I could not keep up with the lessons? I opened the school website again, but it could not answer those questions.

My older sister listened to me. "You've thought carefully about your choice," she said. "But you can't know every part of school life before you begin."

I took out a notebook. Instead of comparing schools again, I wrote down three things I could try: say hello to a classmate, ask a teacher for help when necessary, and attend the science club's first meeting.

The list did not take away all my worries. However, it gave me something to do besides worry. I closed the website and put the notebook in my bag.

variants.advanced:
I finally chose a high school last Friday. It offered a science club I wanted to join, and the bus journey took twenty minutes. Before deciding, I had compared schools, discussed them with my parents, and visited the school. I expected the decision to bring relief, yet some worries remained.

That evening, my best friend said she had chosen a different school. I immediately imagined eating lunch alone. Would everyone else make friends before I did? Would I be able to keep up with the lessons? I returned to the school website, although its pages could not tell me how my own school life would turn out.

My older sister listened without telling me to choose again. "You've considered your choice carefully," she said. "You can't experience every part of a school before you start attending it."

Her words helped me notice the difference between choosing a school and preparing to enter it. I opened a notebook and listed three actions: greet a classmate, ask a teacher for help when necessary, and attend the science club's first meeting.

None of these steps guaranteed an easy first day. They did, however, give me a way to take part in school life instead of only worrying about it. With some questions still unanswered, I closed the website and put the notebook in my bag.
variants.prestudy:
Last Friday, I finally chose a high school that offered a science club I wanted to join. It was a twenty-minute bus ride away. Before reaching my decision, I had compared schools, discussed them with my parents, and visited the school. The decision was informed, but it did not bring the complete relief I had expected.

When my best friend told me that evening that she had chosen another school, I pictured myself eating lunch alone. I also wondered whether I could keep up with the lessons. Returning to the school website, I searched for reassurance. Yet the information there could not predict the friendships I would form or the difficulties I might face.

My older sister listened. Rather than recommending another school, she reminded me that careful preparation could not remove every uncertainty. "You can make a thoughtful choice without knowing exactly how everything will turn out," she said.

I began to distinguish what I could do now from what I could discover only after entering school. In a notebook, I listed three manageable actions: greet a classmate, seek a teacher's help when necessary, and attend the science club's first meeting.

These steps were not a promise that I would never feel lonely or struggle with a lesson. They were opportunities to respond when difficulties arose. Although the uncertainty remained, I no longer treated it as proof that my decision was wrong. I closed the website and put the notebook in my bag.
